_comment: The label taxonomy, and the only place it is written down.
── Namespaces are the sort order
GitHub lists labels alphabetically and offers no way to group them, so the
grouping is spelled into the names: `area/` what it touches, `lang/` what
it is written in, `size/` how much of it moved, `type/` what kind of change
it is, `status/` what a human decided, `topic/` what this repository in
particular argues about. Every dropdown, filter, and pull
request row therefore arrives pre-grouped, and a label's family is legible
from a glance at its color: teal areas, indigo languages, a neutral size
ramp, semantic types, hot statuses.
── A row says how it is earned
`paths` is matched against the pull request's changed files, `commit` against
the conventional-commit type in its title, `from` against the count of
changed lines, and `when` against a fact about an issue. A row with none of
those four is applied by hand and the automation will never touch it — that
is the whole ownership boundary, and `.github/scripts/triage.py` reads it
here rather than restating it.
The boundary narrows by subject too. Only a pull request has a diff and only
an issue can be sitting unread, so `paths` and `from` are never asked of an
issue, `when` is never asked of a pull request, and neither kind of subject
can strip a label the other one earned. An issue therefore takes the type its
title claims when the title happens to be a conventional commit, and
`status/needs-triage` for as long as nobody has classified it — which comes
off by itself the moment a real label lands.
── Glob semantics
The ones .gitignore already taught this tree. A pattern with a `/` matches
the whole path, where `*` stops at a separator and `**` spans them, so
`crates/zoning/src/lsp/**` is that whole subtree while `crates/*.toml` is
only the manifests sitting at that root. A pattern without a `/` matches the
file's name at any depth, so `Cargo.toml` finds both the workspace manifest
and the one under `crates/zoning/` without anybody encoding how deep it sits.
── Areas overlap on purpose
These are a set, not a partition. `area/contract` is the judge itself — the
seven laws, the dialects, and the glob matcher — and `area/cli` is the verbs
and rendering built on top of it; a change that adds a law usually touches
both.
── The bare labels are the issue vocabulary
`bug`, `enhancement`, `question` and their neighbours describe an issue, not
a change, so no `paths`/`commit`/`from` rule can earn one and the automation
never applies them. They are declared anyway, for two reasons: a label this
file does not know about is one GitHub silently drops when a template asks
for it, and undeclared defaults keep GitHub's stock colors, which clash with
the palette below. Living outside every declared namespace is also why
`sync --prune` cannot reach them.
`good first issue` and `help wanted` keep their exact spelling because
GitHub's contributor discovery looks for it.
── Colors have an origin
Each hex is a documented OKLCH coordinate rather than a taste: areas are
oklch(0.62 0.10 195), languages oklch(0.58 0.09 275), the size ramp holds
hue 250 at chroma 0.015 and walks lightness 0.90 → 0.44, and the types carry
the conventional semantics (green feature, red fix, gold performance).
`topic/` is oklch(0.60 0.13 330). The issue vocabulary is paired with the
change types it answers to rather than given a family of its own: `bug` is
a deeper `type/fix` at oklch(0.55 0.18 22), `enhancement` a lighter
`type/feat` at oklch(0.78 0.10 150), and the triage outcomes sit on the
size ramp's neutral hue so a closed-without-a-change reads as quiet.
── The type list is the release contract
These `commit` values are exactly the types `release-please-config.json`
groups its changelog by. A title using anything else fails the triage check,
because the squash commit is what release-please reads.
